This argument is frustrating because it disregards the whole point of encryption. A cryptosystem is only as strong as its weakest link, and a backdoor is very weak.

Cracking a code is difficult because you have to figure out the key, which was chosen at random by the sender. There is an astronomical number of possible keys, and the NSA would have to try them all to decrypt the message. Instead, they want a smaller number of master keys that they can use that will immediately decrypt the message. But now any attackers can just crack the system using the master key instead of the regular key.

Imagine your front door has a combination lock with a trillion possibilities and the backdoor has a lock with a hundred. Any intelligent criminal is going to use the backdoor, so the front door lock is pointless no matter how strong it is.

And of course, if anyone else exploits the backdoor (by cracking it or through a deliberate or accidental leak), it allows them to decrypt everything that has ever been encrypted with the system. Naturally, the NSA wouldn't use the flawed system for their own communication (they're not stupid), so only the civilians they forced to use that system would have their data exposed to the world.

That's assuming the NSA is too incompetent to protect the master key.

For those whom want to make things more difficult, there's multi-phase encryption. It takes a bit longer to do, but it makes things harder to compromise.

Say, for sake of argument, that you have a thumb drive. You encrypt that thumb drive with one kind of encryption. Then there's a folder on that thumb drive, that you encrypt another way. Inside that folder are important documents, each of which are also encrypted using a third method. There are ways to make things far more difficult for people hacking into your system. Sure, it takes more time and isn't nearly as convenient, but it's a great way to step up the game of privacy.
